problems.quote: a power the legislature lacked after the insertion of Article 31A
problems.problem: Article 31A was inserted to confer power on the legislature to acquire property without being challenged under fundamental rights; the legislature lacked this power before, not after, its insertion.
problems.correction: a power the legislature lacked before the insertion of Article 31A
problems.verifierReason: Art 31A inserted 1951 gave legislature power it lacked before; original reverses timeline.

problems.quote: attracted the colourable legislation doctrine
problems.problem: The majority in Puttaswamy (2017) applied the proportionality test, not the doctrine of colourable legislation, which concerns legislative competence, not fundamental rights infringement.
problems.correction: was held to violate the right to privacy
problems.verifierReason: Puttaswamy applied proportionality test for privacy, not colourable legislation doctrine.

problems.quote: The Court applied pith and substance to hold that the amendment’s dominant purpose was to immunise
problems.problem: Minerva Mills (1980) used the basic structure doctrine, not pith and substance (which applies to legislative competence), to strike down the expansion of Article 31C.
problems.correction: The Court applied the basic structure doctrine to hold that the amendment’s dominant purpose was to immunise
problems.verifierReason: Minerva Mills used basic structure doctrine, not pith and substance, to strike down Art 31C expansion.

problems.quote: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) the Court declined to issue a mandamus for the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code
problems.problem: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) concerned GST compensation, not the Uniform Civil Code; the UCC mandamus refusal was in a different case.
problems.correction: the Court in a separate case declined to issue a mandamus for the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code
problems.verifierReason: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) concerned GST compensation, not UCC mandamus.

problems.quote: The Justice J. S. Verma Committee (2013) recommended granting SHRCs independent investigative wings and making their recommendations binding on state governments
problems.problem: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (2013) was constituted for criminal law reforms after the Nirbhaya case; it did not make recommendations on SHRCs.
problems.correction: A separate committee on human rights commissions recommended granting SHRCs independent investigative wings
problems.verifierReason: Justice Verma Committee (2013) was for criminal law reforms, not SHRC recommendations.

problems.quote: relied on NHRC findings to direct compensation for bonded labourers
problems.problem: The NHRC was established in 1993; the cited case (1982) predates it, so the Court could not have relied on NHRC findings.
problems.correction: relied on the findings of a commission of inquiry
problems.verifierReason: NHRC established 1993; 1982 case could not rely on its findings. Correction plausible.

problems.quote: the 103rd Amendment’s 10 % EWS quota only to the extent it violated the 50 % ceiling (Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta, 2018)
problems.problem: The case cited is incorrect. Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) dealt with creamy layer exclusion for SC/ST promotions, not the EWS quota. The 103rd Amendment (2019) was upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022).
problems.correction: the 103rd Amendment’s 10 % EWS quota was upheld as not violating the basic structure (Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, 2022)
problems.verifierReason: Original cites 2018 case for 2019 Amendment; Jarnail Singh dealt with SC/ST creamy layer, not EWS. Correction cites correct 2022 Constitution Bench judgment upholding 103rd Amendment.

problems.quote: The annual Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) convention
problems.problem: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas has been held biennially (every two years) since 2015, not annually.
problems.correction: The biennial Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) convention
problems.verifierReason: PBD was annual 2003-2015; switched to biennial in 2015 per MEA decision.

problems.quote: co‑chaired by the IMF and the World Bank
problems.problem: The Common Framework for Debt Treatments is a G20 initiative supported by the IMF and World Bank, not co‑chaired by them.
problems.correction: a G20 initiative supported by the IMF and the World Bank
problems.verifierReason: Common Framework is G20 initiative, IMF/WB support not co-chair.

problems.quote: DPDP 23 demands dynamic “logic explanations.”
problems.problem: DPDP Act Section 23 does not require logic explanations; it establishes the Data Protection Board.
problems.correction: DPDP Act does not require logic explanations

problems.quote: DPDP’s “reasonable explanation” requirement
problems.problem: The DPDP Act does not contain a “reasonable explanation” requirement.

problems.verifierReason: DPDP Act has no 'reasonable explanation' requirement

problems.quote: DPDP‑mandated logic explanations

problems.verifierReason: DPDP Act does not mandate logic explanations

problems.quote: public hearings under Section 21 of the NGT Act, 2010
problems.problem: Section 21 of the NGT Act deals with appeals to the Supreme Court; public hearings are conducted under the EIA Notification, not the NGT Act.
problems.correction: public hearings under the EIA Notification

problems.quote: Environmental Information Transparency Act” (draft, 2024)

problems.quote: it may refer the matter to a larger bench of the Supreme Court for reconsideration
problems.problem: A High Court cannot refer a matter to a larger bench of the Supreme Court; only the Supreme Court itself can constitute a larger bench to reconsider its own decisions.
problems.correction: it must follow the Supreme Court, as only the Supreme Court can refer its own decisions to a larger bench
problems.verifierReason: High Courts cannot refer matters to a larger bench of the Supreme Court; only the Supreme Court itself can constitute larger benches under Article 145(3).

problems.quote: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Court ordered the closure of polluting industries in the Ganga basin
problems.problem: The 1987 M.C. Mehta case (Oleum gas leak) established absolute liability but did not order closure of Ganga basin industries; those orders came in later Ganga pollution cases.
problems.correction: In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Court established absolute liability for hazardous activities; Ganga basin closures came in later cases
problems.verifierReason: The 1987 M.C. Mehta case (Oleum gas leak) established absolute liability; Ganga basin closure orders were issued in subsequent cases starting 1988.

problems.quote: The 2021 amendment to the Constitution (105th Amendment) restored State power to identify OBCs for reservation in local bodies after the Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in Maratha Reservation Case
problems.problem: The 105th Amendment restored state power to identify SEBCs for education and public employment (Articles 15(4) and 16(4)), not for local bodies. Local bodies OBC reservation is governed by Article 243D(6)/243T(6) and was not affected by the Maratha case.
problems.correction: The 105th Amendment restored State power to identify SEBCs for reservation in education and public employment; local bodies OBC reservation remains under State law per Article 243D(6)/243T(6).
problems.verifierReason: 105th Amendment restored state power for SEBC lists under Arts. 15(4)/16(4) only; local bodies OBC reservation under Arts. 243D(6)/243T(6) was unaffected.

problems.quote: In March 2020, Brazil drew US $1.5 billion under the precautionary line
problems.problem: Brazil never drew from the CRA; the first drawing was by South Africa in July 2022.
problems.correction: No CRA drawing occurred in 2020; the first was South Africa’s 2022 precautionary drawing.
problems.verifierReason: Brazil did not draw from CRA in 2020; first drawing was South Africa's precautionary drawing in July 2022.

problems.quote: The first SB meeting convened in Bonn in June 2022
problems.problem: The first meeting of the Article 6.4 Supervisory Body was held in September 2022, not June 2022.
problems.correction: The first SB meeting convened in Bonn in September 2022
problems.verifierReason: First Article 6.4 Supervisory Body meeting was in September 2022, not June 2022.

problems.quote: The 2023 “Technical Expert Review” of the first BTR cycle highlighted that 38 % of reporting parties had not yet implemented CA accounting
problems.problem: First BTRs are due by end of 2024, so a 2023 review of the first BTR cycle is impossible; the 38% figure is fabricated.

problems.verifierReason: First BTRs due by 31 Dec 2024; no Technical Expert Review of first BTR cycle could occur in 2023.

problems.quote: Panchayats with functional Women’s Component Plan Committees increased spending on nutrition centres by 22 % and reduced open‑defecation rates by 15 %
problems.problem: No such NIRD study exists; 'Women’s Component Plan Committees' is not a standard institutional mechanism, and the precise figures are invented.

problems.verifierReason: Quote cites non-existent committees & precise fabricated figures; correction accurately states no authoritative study supports them.

problems.quote: the 30 % earmarking is routinely met by re‑classifying existing sanitation expenditure without additional services
problems.problem: The 30% earmarking refers to the discontinued Women's Component Plan (1997–2002), not a current gender budgeting requirement for states.

problems.verifierReason: 30% earmarking was Women's Component Plan (1997-2002), not current gender budgeting; correction correctly states it ended in 2002 with no fixed % now.

The basic structure doctrine is a declaration of existing constitut
problems.correction: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the majority established the basic structure doctrine and upheld the validity of the 24th and 29th Amendments while striking down part of the 25th Ame
problems.verifierReason: Original misstates prospective overruling; Court struck down part of 25th Amendment, did not shield past amendments.

problems.quote: In State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) the Court held that a new construction of a tax statute would apply prospectively to avoid hardship to taxpayers who had relied on the earlier interpreta
problems.problem: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) (AIR 1978 SC 68) concerned the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356, not tax statute interpretation. The citation is incorrect for the proposition stated.
problems.correction: In Keshavji Ravji v. CIT (1990) (or similar tax jurisprudence), the Court held that a new construction of a tax statute would apply prospectively to avoid hardship to taxpayers.
problems.verifierReason: State of Karnataka v. Union of India (1977) concerns Art. 356, not tax law; correction cites correct tax case.

problems.quote: The Court also introduced the principle of floor test as a constitutional remedy
problems.problem: The floor test principle was introduced in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), not in Rameshwar Prasad (2006).
problems.correction: The Court applied the floor test principle from Bommai (1994)
problems.verifierReason: Floor test principle originated in Bommai (1994); Rameshwar Prasad (2006) applied it.

problems.quote: The principle was refined in Delhi Laws Act v. Union of India (1951)
problems.problem: Delhi Laws Act (1951) preceded Hamdard Dawakhana (1960); the essential/ancillary distinction was made earlier, not as a refinement of the later doctrine.
problems.correction: The principle was laid down in Delhi Laws Act (1951), not refined later.
problems.verifierReason: Delhi Laws Act (1951) laid down essential/ancillary distinction; not a refinement.
